title: The Potter Who Invented Japanese Porcelain
event_summary: Yi Sam-pyeong, a Korean potter forcibly abducted during Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea in the 1590s, discovered high-quality kaolin clay at Izumiyama quarry near Arita and successfully fired Japan's first true porcelain. His techniques, refined over years of captivity, launched the Arita porcelain industry that would transform global luxury trade. Within decades, millions of pieces were being shipped to Europe through Dutch traders, directly competing with and sometimes replacing Chinese exports disrupted by the Ming-Qing transition.
why_forgotten: Japanese narratives celebrated Arita ware as a national achievement while downplaying its origins in the kidnapping of tens of thousands of Korean artisans — a mass abduction sometimes called the 'Pottery Wars.' Korean contributions were quietly absorbed into Japanese cultural identity, and Yi Sam-pyeong's story survived mainly in local shrine traditions rather than mainstream history. The uncomfortable reality that Japan's most celebrated ceramic tradition was built on forced labor and stolen expertise made both nations reluctant to foreground the story.
why_it_matters: Arita porcelain flooded European markets in the 17th century, inspiring direct imitations at Meissen, Delft, and Sèvres that built Europe's own ceramics industries and reshaped aristocratic material culture. The global demand for porcelain helped establish the Dutch East India Company's trade networks as dominant commercial arteries, shaping early capitalism. Yi Sam-pyeong's discovery also demonstrates how forced migration and war captivity have been hidden engines of technological transfer throughout history — a pattern repeated from Roman-era glassblowing to Cold War rocket science.
